\section[a desilusão]{a desilusão — disappointment}

\label{lesson:PT-C476-desilusao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to calm, then the Portuguese for relief.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a desilusão}
\textbf{a desilusão} — \textquotedblleft{}disappointment\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O concerto foi uma desilusão.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The concert was a disappointment.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Uma desilusão amorosa} — a heartbreak.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desilusão} is built from \emph{des-} and \emph{ilusão} \textquotedblleft{}illusion\textquotedblright{}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{illūsiō} \textquotedblleft{}mockery, deceit\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{lūdere} \textquotedblleft{}to play\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a desilusão}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a desilusão}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a desilusão}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to calm, then the Portuguese for relief, then say \emph{a desilusão} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a desilusão mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Disappointment\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[desiludir]{desiludir — to disappoint, to let down}

\label{lesson:PT-C476-desiludir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for relief, then the Portuguese for disappointment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: desiludir}
\textbf{desiludir} — \textquotedblleft{}to disappoint, to let down\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O filme desiludiu-me: esperava mais.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The film disappointed me: I expected more.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ficar desiludido} — to be disappointed.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desiludir} is built from \emph{des-} and \emph{iludir} \textquotedblleft{}to deceive\textquotedblright{}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{illūdere} \textquotedblleft{}to mock\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{lūdere} \textquotedblleft{}to play\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[desanimado]{desanimado — discouraged, down}

\label{lesson:PT-C476-desanimado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for disappointment, then the Portuguese for to disappoint.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: desanimado}
\textbf{desanimado} — \textquotedblleft{}discouraged, down\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Depois da derrota, a equipa estava desanimada.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After the defeat, the team was down.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Animado} is the opposite: in good spirits.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desanimado} is built from \emph{des-} and \emph{animar} \textquotedblleft{}to cheer up\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{animāre} \textquotedblleft{}to give life to\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{anima} \textquotedblleft{}breath, soul\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[consolar]{consolar — to console, to comfort}

\label{lesson:PT-C476-consolar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to disappoint, then the Portuguese for discouraged.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: consolar}
\textbf{consolar} — \textquotedblleft{}to console, to comfort\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Consolei a minha amiga depois da má notícia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I comforted my friend after the bad news.}
\end{quote}

The noun is \emph{o consolo} — comfort.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{consolar} comes from Latin \emph{cōnsōlārī} \textquotedblleft{}to comfort, to console\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[desabafar]{desabafar — to get something off your chest, to unburden yourself}

\label{lesson:PT-C476-desabafar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for discouraged, then the Portuguese for to console.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: desabafar}
\textbf{desabafar} — \textquotedblleft{}to get something off your chest, to unburden yourself\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Precisava de desabafar e telefonei à minha irmã.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I needed to get it off my chest, so I phoned my sister.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Desabafar com alguém} — to pour your heart out to someone.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desabafar} is usually explained as \emph{des-} plus \emph{abafar} \textquotedblleft{}to smother, to cover\textquotedblright{}: to uncover what was held in. EtymDB lists the word without a source (EtymDB), and the origin of \emph{abafar} is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
